items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: The interviewee mentions Eddie Condon playing with Louis Armstrong and Fats Waller as examples of racial integration in jazz recordings, but does not describe a personal relationship with Condon.

ctx.x: When you were doing this research in your early years of listening, did you start in your mind to be able to categorize things? Like when you heard something did you think of it as New Orleans jazz or Chicago style, or was there a difference between black and white bands for instance that you could hear?

Well there was in the sense that in the earlier days of jazz, black musicians and white musicians tended not to play together in public. And that included phonograph records for quite a while, although as we all know from the memoirs of everybody from © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Armstrong on down, after hours was a different situation. But the division even stayed on records for quite a long time, although it was broken in small ways like Jelly Roll Morton playing with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings on that record in 1922 I believe or ‘23. And that I think happened because Jelly Roll’s music was published by Melrose Brothers in Chicago, and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings also placed publications with Melrose and so it was a natural thing that Jelly Roll would participate in some of these…

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got to know them. Among the things that really impressed me... Eddie Condon, Pee Wee Russell, Jimmy McPartland, Bud Freeman. They were basically the nucleus always of the band down at Nick’s in Greenwich Village. I used to go down to Nick’s a lot. I got to know them.

ctx.x: I guess in maybe 40 years. It will be – things were opened when I came back out of the Army, but even so. I don’t want to even think about that, because I have to have the time to attack this, and I just don’t have time. Life continues to be terribly busy, even though I’m supposed to have been retired for many years. But it’s busy in different ways. We’ll get to that too. Let’s go back to 1939, because I’ve left out one thing that had already started before the trip to California, which took place right after my…

States. There was the Bix Beiderbecke Memorial Album on Victor and the Bessie Smith Memorial Album on Columbia. In England there had been three on British Brunswick. They were devoted to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band – wait a minute. I’m not so sure about that, but let’s set that aside for the moment. But definitely the King Oliver jazz band and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings – that’s right.
